questions.q: State two specific benefits that Indian consumers have experienced due to globalisation since the 1991 reforms.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Greater variety and choice of goods (e.g., multiple brands of smartphones, cars, processed foods) and (2) Lower prices and improved quality due to competition from imported goods and MNCs setting up local production. A wrong answer like "consumers got cheaper goods because imports became tax-free" reveals confusion between globalisation and zero tariffs — India still has tariffs, but they are lower; the benefit comes from competition, not just tariff removal. Another wrong answer "consumers got foreign goods" misses the quality/price dimension and the role of domestic producers improving due to competition.

questions.q: Explain why the entry of Multinational Corporations (MNCs) into the Indian automobile sector after 1991 led to better quality cars for Indian consumers, even for cars produced by Indian companies like Maruti or Tata.
questions.a: Correct answer: MNC entry (e.g., Hyundai, Honda, Ford) introduced new technology, modern production processes, and global quality benchmarks. Indian firms like Maruti (Suzuki joint venture) and Tata had to upgrade their technology, adopt just-in-time inventory, improve worker skills, and meet stricter quality standards to survive the competition. This "competitive pressure" forced a race to the top in quality. A wrong answer like "MNCs brought better cars so Indian companies copied them" misses the systemic mechanism: it is the threat of losing market share that drives continuous upgrading, not one-time copying. Another error: "Government forced Indian companies to improve" — incorrect, the driver was market competition, not regulation.

questions.q: An Indian textile manufacturer in Tirupur used to sell only in domestic markets. After globalisation, they started exporting to Europe. Their revenue increased from ₹50 crore to ₹120 crore in three years. They invested ₹30 crore in new automated dyeing machines imported from Germany. Identify TWO positive effects of globalisation on this producer illustrated by this scenario.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Access to larger international markets (export opportunity) leading to higher revenue and economies of scale. (2) Access to advanced foreign technology (automated dyeing machines from Germany) that improves productivity and quality. Steps: Identify the producer (textile manufacturer). Identify the change: globalisation enabled exports. Effect 1: Revenue jump from ₹50 cr to ₹120 cr shows market access. Effect 2: Import of German machines shows technology access. A wrong answer like "they earned more profit" confuses revenue with profit and misses the structural benefits. Another error: "they got foreign investment" — the scenario shows import of machinery, not FDI.

questions.q: Compare the impact of globalisation on a large Indian IT services firm (e.g., TCS) versus a small traditional handloom weaver in Varanasi. Why does the IT firm benefit more from globalisation in the short run?
questions.a: Correct answer: The IT firm benefits more because its service is digitally tradable, requires high skill (which India has abundantly), faces low transport costs, and can scale globally without physical shipping barriers. The handloom weaver produces a physical good with high per-unit shipping costs, faces intense competition from cheaper machine-made imports, lacks branding/marketing access, and cannot easily meet international quality/packaging standards. Globalisation initially favors sectors where India has comparative advantage (skill-intensive services) over traditional labor-intensive manufacturing with low technology. A wrong answer like "IT firms are bigger so they win" misses the tradability and comparative advantage logic. Another error: "Government supports IT more" — while true, the fundamental reason is economic structure, not policy alone.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Globalisation has been uniformly beneficial for all Indian producers because it opened up export markets." Provide two arguments against this statement using concepts from this chapter.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The statement is false. Argument 1: Small producers (e.g., toy makers, battery manufacturers) faced ruinous competition from cheaper, better-quality imports (especially from China) after tariff reductions, leading to factory closures and job losses — they could not compete due to lack of capital, technology, and scale. Argument 2: Globalisation benefits producers with access to capital, technology, and skilled labor (e.g., pharma, auto parts, IT), but producers in the unorganised sector lack these and are displaced. The gains are uneven — "winners" are export-competitive firms; "losers" are import-competing small firms. A wrong answer like "some producers lost money" is too vague. Must specify the structural reasons: comparative advantage, scale economies, and factor mobility differences.

questions.q: Construct a short scenario (3-4 sentences) showing how globalisation benefited an Indian consumer in a tier-2 city (e.g., Indore, Coimbatore) through a service that was unavailable before 1991. Include the role of technology and competition.
questions.a: Expected answer: Example — "Priya in Coimbatore uses a food delivery app (Zomato/Swiggy) to order Korean, Italian, and local cuisines delivered in 30 minutes. Before 1991, she had only 2-3 local restaurants with no delivery. Globalisation brought foreign capital (e.g., Info Edge, foreign VCs) and technology (GPS, digital payments, cloud kitchens) that enabled platform competition, expanding her choices dramatically." Good answer must include: (1) specific service unavailable pre-1991, (2) role of foreign investment/technology, (3) competition expanding choice. A poor answer like "she can buy imported chocolates" focuses on goods not services, and misses the digital platform revolution driven by global capital and tech.
